kaigo-move-01-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain ADL, IADL and different postures.
Check the person’s wishes, scheduled times and mobility method separately.

kaigo-move-01-knowledge-0.heading: ADL, IADL and the purpose of mobility
paragraphs: Activities of daily living (ADL) are basic actions such as eating, dressing, toileting, bathing and mobility. Instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) support life at home and in the community, including shopping, laundry, managing money, transport and communication devices. One ADL ability does not establish every IADL ability. Check strengths and assistance needs for each activity.

Mobility is more than changing physical location. It supports meaningful participation, such as going to eat in the dining room or talking with others in the activity room. Ask the person about the purpose of going somewhere too.

kaigo-move-01-knowledge-1.heading: Bones, joints, muscles and body regions
paragraphs: Bones support the body and protect internal structures. Joints connecting bones and contracting muscles help produce movement. Shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees and ankles differ in shape and movement. Check pain or difficulty moving particular areas and support them according to the individual plan.

Distinguish body-location terms: head, neck, chest, abdomen, back, lower back, buttocks, arms, elbows, wrists, palms, backs of the hands, legs, knees, ankles, heels and soles. Do not locate pain from “my leg hurts” alone; check where the person points and how they describe it.

kaigo-move-01-knowledge-2.heading: Distinguish standing, sitting and lying
paragraphs: Standing, sitting and lying are different postures. Sitting on the edge of a bed with legs down, sitting in a chair and sitting with legs extended all involve different support conditions.

Lying positions include supine on the back, side-lying and prone on the abdomen. Positions with the upper body raised include Fowler’s and semi-Fowler’s positions. A name alone does not establish stability or the right angle; check the purpose, the person’s condition and the plan.

kaigo-move-01-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Morikawa is sitting stably in a wheelchair, and the individual plan specifies wheelchair travel to the activity room. Before departure, check the time, concerns about the entrance and seating preferences. This situation does not practice transfer techniques.

kaigo-depth-04.heading: Comfortable positioning and cushions
paragraphs: Supine lying supports a broad area of the body, but pressure on bony prominences needs attention. In side-lying, avoid trapping limbs or pressing bony areas directly together. Raising the upper body may allow sliding and pull on the skin. Check pain, breathing, range of movement and skin.

In side-lying, use cushions as needed in front of the chest, around limbs or between the legs to avoid twisting the shoulder, pelvis or knees. With the upper body raised, use the bed’s leg-section functions or a cushion under the knees according to the plan. Raising the head alone does not establish stability.

After raising the upper body, use trained methods for relieving pressure and shear at the back, smooth bedding wrinkles and ask how the person feels. Do not stack thick pillows that bend the neck unnaturally or tightly pack every gap. Select the support areas and continue observing pressure, pain, numbness and skin changes.

[Learning case] A person lying on their side reports knee pain, with both knees directly against each other. Check the painful area and leg positions and support the necessary spacing according to the plan. Do not twist the lower back or knees or ignore pain; check the person’s response afterward too.

This section explains reasons for assistance and what to check. Actual methods depend on the person’s condition, individual plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not attempt unfamiliar transfers or walking assistance from this text alone.

kaigo-move-01-words.heading: Vocabulary and useful expressions
paragraphs: 移動（いどう） — Mobility: moving between places for a purpose in everyday life.
車いす（くるまいす） — Wheelchair: equipment supporting seated mobility. It may be operated by the person or a helper.
声かけ（こえかけ） — Speaking to someone to explain, check, greet or otherwise communicate.
予定表（よていひょう） — Schedule: planned activities and times. Distinguish it from a record of completed actions.
入口（いりぐち） — Entrance: a place to enter a room or building.
支援計画（しえんけいかく） — Support plan: arrangements for support based on the person’s goals and condition.
希望（きぼう） — Wishes: what the person wants to do or have happen.
確認（かくにん） — Checking: clarifying uncertainty by asking or observing directly.
ADL（エー・ディー・エル） — Basic activities of daily living, such as eating, dressing, toileting, bathing and mobility.
IADL（アイ・エー・ディー・エル） — Activities supporting life at home and in the community, such as shopping, money management and transport.
移乗（いじょう） — Transfer: changing the surface supporting the body, such as moving from bed to wheelchair.
移動用リフト（いどうようりふと） — Patient lift: equipment supporting and lifting the body to assist transfers. Check suitability and the trained method of use.
起き上がる（おきあがる） — To sit up: raising the upper body from lying toward sitting.
かける（かける） — In “apply the brakes,” this means activating the brakes to keep something stopped.
臥床（がしょう） — Lying in bed or on a similar surface.
支える（ささえる） — To support: providing the support needed to keep a body or object stable.
シルバーカー（しるばーかー） — A walking cart for older people. Check each product’s purpose; do not assume it is a wheelchair.
高齢者用手押し車（こうれいしゃようておしぐるま） — A cart pushed by an older person. Check the product’s intended use rather than inferring from its name whether it can carry someone.
すべる（すべる） — To slide or slip: moving over a contacting surface, or losing secure footing.
スライディングシート（すらいでぃんぐしーと） — Sliding sheet: a sheet used to reduce friction when moving the body.
杖（つえ） — Cane: an aid providing additional support while walking. Check type and suitability.
つく（つく） — In “place a cane,” this means putting its tip on the floor or ground for support.
つかまる（つかまる） — To hold a rail or similar support to steady the body.
手すり（てすり） — Handrail: a fixture held for support when standing or walking.
握る（にぎる） — To grip: holding something by bending the fingers around it.
寝返り（ねがえり） — Turning over while lying down.
白杖（はくじょう） — White cane: used by a person with visual impairment to check surroundings and for related purposes. Respect their method of use.
ブレーキ（ぶれーき） — Brake: a device stopping or limiting wheel movement. Distinguish the roles and use of different types.
歩行器（ほこうき） — Walker: equipment supporting the body during walking. Check its type and use.
前屈み（まえかがみ） — Forward-leaning posture. The suitable degree depends on the person and action.
誘導（ゆうどう） — Guiding: explaining direction and path conditions according to the person’s wishes and condition.
床（ゆか） — Floor: a supporting surface in a room or passage. Check for moisture and objects.
離床（りしょう） — Getting out of bed to sit or take part in activities, according to the person’s condition and plan.
介護職（かいごしょく） — Care work: providing necessary daily assistance while respecting the person’s abilities and decisions.
Useful expression: Let’s look at the schedule together. It starts at two, so we still have fifteen minutes.
Useful expression: I’ll check the entrance. If it’s crowded, let’s wait a little before going in.

kaigo-move-01-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Morikawa is sitting stably in a wheelchair, and the individual plan specifies wheelchair travel to the activity room. Before departure, check the time, concerns about the entrance and seating preferences. This situation does not practice transfer techniques.
Haruko Morikawa: I’d like to join the afternoon gathering, but I want to check the time before leaving my room.
Care worker Tanaka: Let’s look at the schedule together. It starts at two, so we still have fifteen minutes.
Haruko Morikawa: There’s no need to rush, then. I’m going by wheelchair today, aren’t I?
Care worker Tanaka: Yes, that’s the current support plan. Is anything worrying you before we go?
Haruko Morikawa: I’m a little worried about bumping into people at the entrance.
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll check the entrance. If it’s crowded, let’s wait a little before going in.
Haruko Morikawa: All right. I’d like to sit near the window when we get there.
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll check for a seat near the window. May we start moving now?
Haruko Morikawa: Yes, please.
Care worker Tanaka: Let’s go to the entrance together. Please tell me if you’d like to stop along the way.

kaigo-move-01-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] The person wants to attend an activity, but the mobility method for this time is unknown. Whether a window seat is available is also unconfirmed.

Listen to the person’s wishes and check the planned method with the person responsible. Explain the method and preparations and check consent before arranging them. Do not choose a wheelchair solely for staff convenience or promise an unconfirmed seat.
Example: “I understand you’d like to go. I’ll check the mobility method for this time and the window seat. May I tell you what I find out before we prepare?”
Reflection: Did you distinguish confirmed methods and seat availability from wishes and assumptions?

kaigo-move-01-reading.heading: Read a learning document
paragraphs:
Activity room schedule
Start: 2 p.m.
Entry is available from 1:40 p.m. If the entrance is crowded, wait for the assigned worker’s guidance.

kaigo-language-transfer-209.heading: Read today’s equipment preference
paragraphs: Person receiving care: “I’d like to use the walker today, not yesterday’s cane.” Care worker: “I’ll check the walker preparations.”
Check: What does the person want to use today? Is yesterday’s choice enough to decide today’s equipment?
Reasoning: The person wants a walker and does not want yesterday’s cane today. Acknowledge the current preference and check the plan and preparations rather than assuming they are unchanged.

kaigo-move-02-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain wheelchair parts and the reasons for checking them.
Distinguish who checks the route from who explains it to the person when handing over.

kaigo-move-02-knowledge-0.heading: Choose equipment by purpose and function
paragraphs: Canes provide extra walking support and include T-shaped and multiple-point types. Walkers provide a wider base of support than canes, but functions differ by type. Sliding sheets reduce friction; lifts raise and support the body for transfers. Floor-mobile and ceiling-mounted types exist. Check the person’s condition, equipment fit and instructions.

A walking cart is not automatically a wheelchair for carrying someone just because of its name or a built-in seat. Follow the product’s intended use. Fall prevention involves not just the route but also the person’s condition, footwear, equipment and assistance arrangements.

kaigo-move-02-knowledge-1.heading: Wheelchair inspection and foot-space safety
paragraphs: Wheelchair parts include push handles, arm and back supports, seat, drive wheels, casters, brakes and foot supports. Check tires and brakes before use. Underinflated tires may reduce parking-brake effectiveness. Do not continue using faulty equipment.

Apply parking brakes when stopped, even with nobody seated. Before transfers, move foot supports out of the way using the method for that model. Standing on footplates can cause falls. Support the feet during travel so they do not drag on the floor.

kaigo-move-02-knowledge-2.heading: Check passages, steps and slopes
paragraphs: Crowded entrances, objects, thresholds, changes in level and slopes affect wheelchair movement and stability. Check the route and explain changes to the person. Before moving, check that limbs or clothing cannot become caught in wheels and explain what will happen.

Steps and slopes require different operations from level ground. Knowing part names does not establish operating skill. Consider the wheelchair, surface and gradient, the person’s condition and the helper’s skill, and use trained methods. If conditions are unsuitable, consider another route or further help.

kaigo-move-02-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Objects are in front of the elevator, and the wheelchair has not yet reached them. Tanaka checks another route; Kishimoto explains the change to the person and contacts the destination. This dialogue does not teach wheelchair operation.

kaigo-depth-11.heading: Wheelchair parts and reasons for inspection
paragraphs: The back support and seat support the trunk; arm supports support the arms. Leg supports support the lower legs and foot supports the feet. Handrims on the drive wheels allow self-propulsion; helpers use push handles. Casters are front wheels involved in direction.

Parking brakes hold the wheelchair stationary and differ from helper-operated brakes at the push handles. The tipping lever is used in trained operations such as lifting the front wheels; it is not a boarding step. Push handles do not establish the person’s self-propulsion ability.

Before use, check tires, brake effectiveness and secured parts according to the model. Apply parking brakes when stopped, even unoccupied. Move foot supports out of the transfer path; do not stand on footplates. After seating, support the feet and check that hands and clothing are clear of wheels.

[Learning case] The wheelchair seems likely to move despite applied parking brakes. Do not judge by lever position alone; inspect tires and brakes. Do not compensate for faulty equipment by gripping the push handles harder and continuing to use it.

kaigo-move-02-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Objects are in front of the elevator, and the wheelchair has not yet reached them. Tanaka checks another route; Kishimoto explains the change to the person and contacts the destination. This dialogue does not teach wheelchair operation.
Misaki Kishimoto: There are objects in the corridor to the activity room. May we use another route?
Care worker Tanaka: First, please tell me exactly where the objects are.
Misaki Kishimoto: In front of the elevator. I think it’s too narrow for the wheelchair.
Care worker Tanaka: Please don’t force your way through a narrow space. I’ll check the route now.
Misaki Kishimoto: I’ve asked Morikawa to wait until the check is finished.
Care worker Tanaka: I’ve checked. The right-hand passage is clear, and we can reach the activity room that way.
Misaki Kishimoto: The right-hand passage, then. I’ll explain the route change to Morikawa before we move.
Care worker Tanaka: Please do. Once you arrive, tell the person responsible for the room too.
Misaki Kishimoto: I’ll tell them after arrival. Is there anything else to check?
Care worker Tanaka: Nothing else at present. If a new issue arises, check it at the time.

kaigo-move-02-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] A colleague reports an obstructed area. Another passage has not been checked, and Tanaka agrees to check it.
Agree who will check and report the result, then confirm who explains to the person and contacts the destination. Do not confuse the route checker with the person providing guidance.
Example: “I’ll check the right-hand passage first and report back. Could you then explain it to the person and contact the destination, Kishimoto?”
Reflection: Did you mistake a requested check for confirmation that the passage was safe?

kaigo-move-02-reading.heading: Read a learning document
paragraphs:
Route message
At 1:50 p.m., transport items were in front of the elevator. Care worker Tanaka checked the right-hand passage. Explain the route change to the person before moving.

kaigo-language-transfer-211.heading: Separate destination wishes from equipment readiness
paragraphs: Person receiving care: “I’d like to watch birds in the garden this afternoon.” Care worker: “The wheelchair is in the room. Let’s check before leaving.”
Check: Where does the person want to go, and for what purpose? Does a wheelchair being in the room prove readiness to leave?
Reasoning: The wish is to watch birds in the garden that afternoon. Equipment location alone does not establish its inspection, the person’s condition or required help. Pre-departure checks remain.

kaigo-move-04-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Check explanation, consent, current condition and staffing before assistance.
Distinguish turning over from sitting up and explain checks after changing position.

kaigo-move-04-knowledge-0.heading: Checks before assistance
paragraphs: Before assistance, check current condition and movements the person can perform, explain the purpose and actions, and obtain consent. Arrange the environment, equipment, staffing and roles. If the person is unwell, do not force progress; report to healthcare professionals or other necessary contacts.

A bed height comfortable for the worker reduces lower-back strain. When the person sits at the bed edge, however, check a height allowing both soles to be properly supported on the floor or another suitable surface. The purpose changes by stage, so one height may not suit them all.

kaigo-move-04-knowledge-1.heading: Turning over versus sitting up
paragraphs: Turning over changes direction while lying, such as from supine to side-lying. Sitting up raises the upper body from lying and requires coordinated trunk and leg movement. In the example involving hemiplegia, protect the affected shoulder and arm and use retained strength.

Do not move the body by pulling a paralyzed arm or rubbing skin forcefully against bedding. Preserve actions the person can perform and support the trunk and other areas using trained methods suited to their condition.

kaigo-move-04-knowledge-2.heading: Checks after repositioning
paragraphs: After turning, check for a trapped arm, twisted legs or pelvis, pain or discomfort. After sitting up, check how the person feels, dizziness, foot support and sitting stability.

“Sitting” in a plan or an upright upper body does not prove stable sitting. Do not proceed to standing while unstable. Hand placement, force and coordination between helpers require supervised practical checks separate from understanding the text.

kaigo-move-04-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Tanaka is supporting Hasebe at this time of day for the first time. Standing, walking and transfer have not happened. Read the individual message and check the current condition with assigned worker Kishimoto before beginning.

kaigo-depth-06.heading: Coordinate trunk and limbs when turning
paragraphs: Turning over coordinates shoulders, trunk, pelvis and legs while avoiding skin pulling and twisting. The course example involving hemiplegia uses side-lying with the affected side uppermost. It does not require everyone with hemiplegia to lie in the same direction.

Check condition, pain and range of movement; arrange explanation and consent, bed height and space. Use the person’s retained movement and position the knees and other parts within their abilities. Coordinate trunk and pelvis at trained support points rather than suddenly pulling one limb to move the whole body.

After turning, position and stabilize the pelvis and legs and support necessary gaps. Check shoulder strain, trapped arms, proximity to the bed edge and comfort. If new pain or difficulty appears, check and seek advice rather than applying more force.

[Learning case] After turning, the affected arm remains under the chest and the legs are twisted. “Turn completed” does not justify moving on. Maintain safe support, check and adjust limb positions, pain and skin, and obtain needed help.

kaigo-depth-07.heading: Sitting up and stability at the bed edge
paragraphs: Moving from side-lying to sitting at the bed edge changes the support surface. The source example combines lowering both legs beyond the bed edge with raising the upper body using the stronger elbow. It does not describe pulling someone upright by the arms or neck.

Protect the affected shoulder and arm, check planned supports and coordinate trunk and legs. Adjust bed height so both soles are properly supported when seated at the edge. Do not apply this method unchanged to someone unable to use their elbow for support.

After sitting, separately check well-being, condition, dizziness, expression, foot support and balance. A height convenient for the helper may leave the person’s feet unsupported. Sitting up does not establish readiness to stand immediately.

[Learning case] The upper body is upright, but the feet do not reach the floor and the person feels dizzy. Maintain safe sitting support and postpone the transfer. Check foot support and condition and inform the responsible worker or healthcare professional.

kaigo-move-04-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Tanaka is supporting Hasebe at this time of day for the first time. Standing, walking and transfer have not happened. Read the individual message and check the current condition with assigned worker Kishimoto before beginning.
Naoto Kawase: Can you support Hasebe’s mobility today?
Care worker Tanaka: I can take the assignment, but I haven’t checked the support method for this time. Could we look at the plan together?
Naoto Kawase: Yes. At this time, two assigned workers provide the support.
Care worker Tanaka: Two workers, then. Who is the other person?
Naoto Kawase: Kishimoto. Check the current condition before starting too.
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll speak to Kishimoto and explain to Hasebe that we’ll both check before accompanying them.
Naoto Kawase: Please do. Let me know before starting if their condition differs from the plan.
Care worker Tanaka: Understood. I won’t begin alone; we’ll complete the necessary checks first.

kaigo-move-04-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] The individual plan requires two workers at this time, but only one is preparing.
Identify the other worker and confirm the person’s current condition and support needs together before starting. Do not begin alone or generalize this example to every mobility task.
Example: “The plan specifies two workers at this time. Who is the other worker? We’ll check the current condition together before starting.”
Reflection: Could you explain the need to check roles and current condition, not just staffing numbers?

kaigo-move-04-reading.heading: Read a learning document
paragraphs:
Today’s message
At this time, Hasebe’s mobility requires Kishimoto and another assigned worker. Check the current condition before starting. Consult Kawase if anything differs from the plan.

kaigo-language-transfer-210.heading: Distinguish completed and requested actions
paragraphs: Person receiving care: “I’ve put my jacket on myself. Please help only with the shoes.” Care worker: “The shoes, then. I’ll check how to help.”
Check: What is already completed independently, and what assistance is requested?
Reasoning: The jacket is already on; help is requested only with shoes. Shoe assistance is not reported complete. Check the method without extending assistance to the jacket.

kaigo-move-03-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain standing, comfortable positioning and their relationships with disuse syndrome and pressure injuries.
Report observations, the person’s words, actions and unknowns separately to nursing staff.

kaigo-move-03-knowledge-0.heading: Standing and shifting the center of gravity
paragraphs: Standing from sitting involves foot support and shifting the center of gravity. Appropriate forward movement of the upper body helps transfer weight toward the feet. Pulling the person’s arms cannot replace this coordination.

Check available strength, pain, equipment and the plan. If condition changes during assistance, prioritize safety over finishing on schedule. Pause the next action and involve the responsible worker or healthcare professional.

kaigo-move-03-knowledge-1.heading: Ask the person about comfort
paragraphs: Comfort in supine, side-lying or upper-body-raised positions depends on the person’s condition and support. Cushions can fill support gaps or avoid direct pressure between body areas. Appearance alone does not establish a good posture.
Knowing the name Fowler’s position does not justify the same angle for everyone. Follow the plan and check pain, breathing, skin pressure and comfort.

kaigo-move-03-knowledge-2.heading: Reduced activity, disuse syndrome and pressure injuries
paragraphs: Prolonged rest or reduced activity can cause loss of strength, joint contracture, bone atrophy and reduced cardiopulmonary, sensory or mental function. These changes are called disuse syndrome. Reduced blood-pressure regulation, feeling unwell on standing and nutrition problems can also affect life. A request for a brief rest does not establish this syndrome.

Pressure injuries involve damage to skin and other tissues when sustained pressure impairs blood flow, often over bony areas. Friction and shear against bedding also matter. Combine suitable activity, pressure relief, repositioning, skin checks and nutrition in the individual plan. A uniform repositioning schedule alone does not guarantee prevention.

kaigo-move-03-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person asks to rest at the activity-room entrance. Practice reporting to nursing staff, not diagnosing fatigue or deciding treatment.

kaigo-depth-05.heading: Skin observations and pressure relief
paragraphs: Sustained pressure over bony areas can restrict blood flow and lead to pressure injuries. Consider friction, shear and bedding wrinkles too. Observe according to posture and contact points: the back of the head, shoulder blades, elbows, sacrum and heels in supine lying, and buttocks in sitting. One unchanged area does not establish safety elsewhere.

Observe skin during dressing, hygiene or repositioning and record location, color, pain and changes. Combine possible activity and getting out of bed, planned pressure relief and repositioning, bedding and support surfaces, and nutrition checks. Do not impose one schedule without checking movement ability, skin and equipment.

Report redness or wounds to healthcare professionals for assessment. Do not independently grade the injury or apply medication. Rubbing a red area firmly is not pressure relief. A cushion feeling soft does not prove adequate pressure relief either.

[Learning case] A heel becomes red after prolonged supine lying. Even if the sacrum is unchanged, record the heel finding, check support and pressure, and inform healthcare professionals. Share changes when noticed rather than waiting for a wound.

kaigo-depth-08.heading: Check stability after standing too
paragraphs: Standing up shifts the center of gravity over the feet and raises the upper body. Sitting too deeply or placing feet too far forward can hinder weight transfer. The source example of someone with hemiplegia who can stand uses the unaffected leg and support against affected-knee buckling.

Check chair or bed, floor, footwear, foot position and help needed; adjust sitting position and forward lean within the person’s abilities. Coordinate with trained supports and cues. The source places the worker on the affected side, watching knee buckling, without forcefully pushing the knee or pulling arms.

After standing, check well-being and balance. One successful stand does not establish prolonged standing, turning or clothing management. Consider another method if weight cannot be supported. For dizziness, new pain or knee buckling, pause the next action, maintain safety and seek help.

[Learning case] The person has stood but keeps bent knees and holds a rail. Asking them to release it to pull up trousers may remove support. Prioritize stability and planned help rather than judging by the completed stand alone.

kaigo-move-03-words.heading: Vocabulary and useful expressions

車いす（くるまいす） — Wheelchair: equipment supporting seated mobility. It may be operated by the person or a helper.
声かけ（こえかけ） — Speaking to someone to explain, check, greet or otherwise communicate.
入口（いりぐち） — Entrance: a place to enter a room or building.
未確認（みかくにん） — Unconfirmed: not yet checked. It does not mean no problem exists.
担当（たんとう） — Responsibility for supporting a person or carrying out assigned work.
確認（かくにん） — Checking: clarifying uncertainty by asking or observing directly.
連絡（れんらく） — Passing necessary information to the appropriate recipient.
廃用症候群（はいようしょうこうぐん） — Disuse syndrome: decline in various mental and physical functions associated with prolonged inactivity or reduced activity.
褥瘡（じょくそう） — Pressure injury: damage to skin or underlying tissues associated with sustained pressure and impaired blood flow.
移乗（いじょう） — Transfer: changing the surface supporting the body, such as moving from bed to wheelchair.
移動用リフト（いどうようりふと） — Patient lift: equipment supporting and lifting the body to assist transfers. Check suitability and the trained method of use.
起き上がる（おきあがる） — To sit up: raising the upper body from lying toward sitting.
かける（かける） — In “apply the brakes,” this means activating the brakes to keep something stopped.
臥床（がしょう） — Lying in bed or on a similar surface.
支える（ささえる） — To support: providing the support needed to keep a body or object stable.
シルバーカー（しるばーかー） — A walking cart for older people. Check each product’s purpose; do not assume it is a wheelchair.
高齢者用手押し車（こうれいしゃようておしぐるま） — A cart pushed by an older person. Check the product’s intended use rather than inferring from its name whether it can carry someone.
すべる（すべる） — To slide or slip: moving over a contacting surface, or losing secure footing.
スライディングシート（すらいでぃんぐしーと） — Sliding sheet: a sheet used to reduce friction when moving the body.
杖（つえ） — Cane: an aid providing additional support while walking. Check type and suitability.
つく（つく） — In “place a cane,” this means putting its tip on the floor or ground for support.
つかまる（つかまる） — To hold a rail or similar support to steady the body.
手すり（てすり） — Handrail: a fixture held for support when standing or walking.
握る（にぎる） — To grip: holding something by bending the fingers around it.
寝返り（ねがえり） — Turning over while lying down.

kaigo-move-03-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person asks to rest at the activity-room entrance. Practice reporting to nursing staff, not diagnosing fatigue or deciding treatment.
Aya Fujino: Was there any change during Morikawa’s move?
Care worker Tanaka: At 1:55, when we reached the entrance, Morikawa said, “I’d like a short rest.”
Aya Fujino: What did you do next?
Care worker Tanaka: I paused the move and contacted the assigned worker. Morikawa is waiting while still seated.
Aya Fujino: Did Morikawa mention pain or breathlessness?
Care worker Tanaka: I haven’t heard those concerns, but I haven’t checked them in detail yet.
Aya Fujino: It’s important not to treat unchecked information as absent. Let’s check their condition together now.
Care worker Tanaka: Yes. I’ll wait without restarting the move.
Aya Fujino: Record what was checked and when too. We’ll decide the necessary response after checking their condition.
Care worker Tanaka: Understood. I’ll record confirmed facts separately from the person’s words.

kaigo-move-03-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] At the entrance, the person asks to rest. Pain and breathlessness have not yet been checked in detail.
Pause movement and maintain safety. Report the time, place, person’s words, actions and unknowns. Do not diagnose disuse syndrome from a short rest or press ahead for the schedule.

Example: “At 1:55 p.m. at the activity-room entrance, the person said they wanted to rest. I stopped and contacted the assigned worker. Pain and breathlessness are unconfirmed, so please check their condition.”
Reflection: Did you report unchecked information as absence of symptoms? For sudden changes, follow the facility’s emergency procedures.

kaigo-move-03-reading.heading: Read a learning document

Mobility record
1:55 p.m.: At the activity-room entrance, the person requested rest. Movement paused; assigned worker contacted. Pain and breathlessness unconfirmed. A check with nursing staff is planned.

kaigo-language-transfer-233.heading: Separate comfort from environmental information
paragraphs: Person receiving care: “The chair feels just right.” Care worker: “I understand. However, the floor by your feet is wet. I’ll check what needs to be done first.”
Check: Does a comfortable chair prove that the floor is safe too?
Reasoning: No. Comfort in the chair and a wet floor are separate information. Respect the person’s experience while checking the floor response before moving.

kaigo-move-05-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Explain conditions to check for cane walking, level changes and guiding someone with visual impairment.
Distinguish the current choice not to join from conditions for joining later.

kaigo-move-05-knowledge-0.heading: Two-stage and three-stage cane walking
paragraphs: Consider a person with hemiplegia for whom cane walking is suitable. One method uses the stronger hand. In a three-stage pattern, move the cane, affected leg and unaffected leg separately. In a two-stage pattern, advance the cane and affected leg together, then the unaffected leg.

In the course comparison, three stages allow support to be checked more easily and provide greater stability than two. Do not switch to two stages independently for speed. Provide support from a trained position, such as diagonally behind the affected side. Check cane type, height, weight-bearing conditions and the individual method.

kaigo-move-05-knowledge-1.heading: Distinguish stair ascent from descent
paragraphs: In the source’s hemiplegia-and-cane example, going up means placing the cane, then raising the unaffected leg and affected leg. Going down uses cane, affected leg, unaffected leg. The reminder “up with the stronger leg” does not replace cane placement or preparations.

The worker supports from the lower step: behind on ascent and in front on descent. Check how a handrail is used if present. This is a conditional source example, not instructions for every injury or device. Check suitability of stairs, assistance needs and the plan.

kaigo-move-05-knowledge-2.heading: Information for someone with visual impairment
paragraphs: First identify yourself and your position and ask how the person wants guidance. Have them hold the supporting arm using their preferred method, and walk slightly ahead at their pace. Do not suddenly pull their hand or push their back.

Explain steps, corners, narrow doors and floor changes before reaching them. Agree on a reference such as the person’s perspective rather than saying only “this way.” Prioritize their ability to anticipate and adjust over passing quickly.

kaigo-move-05-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Onodera is sitting stably and wants to wait for a younger sister’s call. The activity is optional, with no urgent need to move. Do not require participation; check present wishes and conditions for joining after the call.

kaigo-depth-09.heading: Keep cane-walking and stair sequences distinct
paragraphs: In the source’s cane-walking example with hemiplegia, three-stage level walking separates cane, affected leg and unaffected leg. Two-stage walking advances cane and affected leg together, then the unaffected leg. Three stages provide more support-checking opportunities and greater stability. Do not change patterns for speed alone.

The stair example uses cane, unaffected leg, affected leg upward and cane, affected leg, unaffected leg downward. The worker stays on the lower-step side, behind on ascent and in front on descent. Rail use and equipment handling also depend on the person and individual instruction.

“Stronger leg up, affected leg down” describes only the order of the legs. It does not replace cane placement, equipment choice or suitability for stairs. Reciting the order does not demonstrate actual support and balance.

kaigo-move-05-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Onodera is sitting stably and wants to wait for a younger sister’s call. The activity is optional, with no urgent need to move. Do not require participation; check present wishes and conditions for joining after the call.
Fumi Onodera: I don’t want to go to the activity room now.
Care worker Tanaka: You’d prefer not to join right now. If you don’t mind, could you tell me why?
Fumi Onodera: My younger sister is going to call, so I’d like to wait here.
Care worker Tanaka: You’d like to wait for the call. May I tell the activity coordinator that you won’t join right now?
Fumi Onodera: Yes. I’d like to know whether I can still join once the call is over.
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll check whether you can join later and let you know as soon as I find out.
Fumi Onodera: Thank you. I’ll wait here until you’ve checked.
Care worker Tanaka: Of course. Let’s decide whether to go after I’ve told you what I find out.

kaigo-move-05-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] The person wants to wait for a call and does not seem to want to explain details now. The activity is optional.

Respect the limited choice not to go now. Do not treat it as an all-day absence; ask only what is needed if they wish to join later. Do not require an explanation as a condition for participation or assistance.
Example: “You’d like to wait now. You don’t have to explain the details. Would you like me to check whether you could join after the call and let you know?”
Reflection: Did you separate the current choice, later participation conditions and consent to sharing information?

kaigo-language-transfer-212.heading: Check a repeated sequence
paragraphs: Care worker: “This practice card uses A, C, B.” Person receiving care: “A, B, C, then.” Care worker: “The second item is C.”
Check: Is the repeated order correct? Give the card’s order.
Reasoning: The correct order is A, C, B. The second item is C, not B. This card practices reading a sequence; it is not instructions for actual cane walking or another procedure or movement.

kaigo-move-06-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Distinguish pre-transfer preparations, post-transfer posture checks and the start of travel.
Accurately hand over a confirmed deadline and the person’s undecided wishes.

kaigo-move-06-knowledge-0.heading: Transfers change the supporting surface
paragraphs: A bed-to-wheelchair transfer differs from pushing a wheelchair. The supporting surface changes, so prepare bed and chair position and height, brakes, foot supports, foot placement and helpers.

The source gives an example for a person with hemiplegia who can stand and turn, placing the chair on the unaffected side to use retained strength. Hemiplegia alone does not justify the same method for everyone. Consider a lift or another method for someone unable to support their weight.

kaigo-move-06-knowledge-1.heading: Checks after sitting and before moving
paragraphs: After transfer, check stable sitting, foot support, hands and clothing clear of wheels, and pain or changes in well-being. Being seated alone does not establish readiness to travel.
Tell the person before movement, then release brakes to proceed. Apply brakes when stopped. Steps and slopes require different skills and checks, not simply faster or harder pushing.

kaigo-move-06-knowledge-2.heading: Hand over completed actions and unknowns
paragraphs: A handoff specifies the activity, assistance level, equipment, person’s words and feelings, and check results. Preparing the wheelchair, completing the transfer and checking the final posture are separate facts.

State unknowns and identify who checks what next. Knowing a joining deadline does not establish a decision to participate. Separate times, conditions and choices so the recipient does not act on assumptions.

kaigo-move-06-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Hand over to Kishimoto about an optional activity. Joining is confirmed possible until 2:30 p.m., but the call’s ending time and the person’s choice are undecided. This situation contains no sudden symptoms or health-related cause.

kaigo-depth-12.heading: Pre-transfer conditions and post-transfer checks
paragraphs: The source transfer example uses the unaffected side for a person with hemiplegia who can stand and turn. It is not directly applicable to someone unable to bear their weight. Check current abilities and the plan; use a lift or other equipment or methods if needed.

Position the wheelchair appropriately, apply effective brakes and move foot supports out of the foot path. Check seat height, foot placement and staffing. Combine the person’s usable hand and support points with trained protection for areas such as the affected knee. Coordinate trunk and legs for turning and support slow sitting.

After sitting, check depth, stability, limb positions, pain and well-being. The worker must not twist only at the waist or have the person hang from their neck. Effective brakes do not justify transfer when distance, height, foot space or condition are unsuitable.

[Learning case] The wheelchair is stopped, but a footplate remains in the path and dizziness continues. Preparations and condition are not ready. Do not proceed; arrange equipment appropriately for the model and report dizziness to the responsible worker or healthcare professional.

kaigo-depth-13.heading: Check conditions for wheelchair steps and slopes
paragraphs: Even on level ground, check foot support and hands clear of wheels, and tell the person before moving. Steps change wheel support, and slopes pull the chair downward. Forward pushing in the same manner does not suit every surface.

In the source example of a low upward step, stop and explain first, control and raise the front wheels using the tipping lever and handles, then raise the rear wheels. On descent, move backward, slowly lower the rear wheels, then control and lower the front wheels. Suitable equipment, surface and training are prerequisites.

The source’s steep-downhill example uses backward travel to prevent forward sliding, checking behind and a staggered foot position for the worker. Backward travel does not make every slope passable. Gradient, chair type and both people’s conditions may require another route or extra help.

Parking brakes are not for controlling speed during travel. Do not skip stopping, explaining or checking the route to save time, or jerk the chair upward with the tipping lever. Do not enter an uncontrollable slope to test whether arm strength can stop it.

kaigo-move-06-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Hand over to Kishimoto about an optional activity. Joining is confirmed possible until 2:30 p.m., but the call’s ending time and the person’s choice are undecided. This situation contains no sudden symptoms or health-related cause.
Misaki Kishimoto: Is there anything to hand over about Onodera’s plans?
Care worker Tanaka: Onodera won’t join the two o’clock activity right now. They want to wait for their younger sister’s call.
Misaki Kishimoto: What is planned after the call?
Care worker Tanaka: The coordinator confirmed joining is possible until two thirty. I’ve told Onodera too.
Misaki Kishimoto: Have they already decided to join?
Care worker Tanaka: It isn’t decided yet. We’ll ask again what they want after the call.
Misaki Kishimoto: I’ll ask after the call, then. Where is the record?
Care worker Tanaka: In today’s activity record. I recorded the joining deadline separately from the unconfirmed participation wish.

kaigo-move-06-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] The joining deadline is confirmed as 2:30 p.m., but the call’s ending time and the later participation choice remain unknown.
Pass on the confirmed deadline, unknowns, next worker and record location. Do not promise the call will finish in time or that the person will definitely join.

Example: “Joining is confirmed possible until 2:30 p.m. The call’s ending time and participation choice remain unknown. Kishimoto, please check their wishes after the call and record them in the handoff section.”
Reflection: Are the message time and joining deadline separate, and is responsibility for the next check clear?

kaigo-language-transfer-253.heading: Distinguish before use, before transfer and afterward
paragraphs: Before use: check brakes and tires. Before transfer: check stopping and preparations. Afterward: record the condition.
Check: Does a completed final record permit omitting pre-use inspection?
Reasoning: No. Brake and tire checks before use, stopping and preparations before transfer, and recording afterward are separate stages. Records must be based on actual checks.

kaigo-move-07-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals

kaigo-move-07-knowledge-0.heading: Combine goals with current conditions
paragraphs: Assistance levels depend on wishes, current abilities, condition, environment, equipment and the individual plan. Wanting to walk independently does not establish safe walking today if the person is dizzy.
Check changes and consult the necessary people about available methods. Safety checks help connect life goals to suitable support rather than justify ignoring wishes.

kaigo-move-07-knowledge-1.heading: Principles and practical verification are separate
paragraphs: The base of support is the area enclosed by the points supporting the body. Understanding its relation to the center of gravity helps explain stability and worker strain. Good posture alone does not authorize lifting another person’s whole weight alone. Arrange equipment, staffing and training too.

Distinguish knowing principles, explaining reasons and operating correctly. Reciting cane order or why brakes matter does not demonstrate force, hand placement, coordination or balance; check these in supervised practice.

kaigo-move-07-knowledge-2.heading: Prior and subsequent checks and near misses
paragraphs: During review, go beyond “report to the person responsible” to explain what is checked before and after and why. Pre-assistance condition, environment and equipment differ in purpose from final posture, well-being and outcome checks.

Share near misses such as a wheelchair almost moving without injury. Record confirmed facts and unknowns. Do not blame one person without checking; review equipment, surroundings, communication and procedures as a team to prevent recurrence.

kaigo-move-07-knowledge-3.heading: Practice situation and limits of assistance

kaigo-depth-10.heading: Advance information when guiding someone with visual impairment
paragraphs: Explain touch, direction and route changes in advance so the person can anticipate movement. Ask how they prefer guidance, have them hold an appropriately positioned arm, and walk slightly ahead at their pace. Do not grab the wrist and pull or push from behind.

Identify your position, check consent and maintain contact through the chosen method. Explain features and directions before corners, steps, narrow doors and floor changes so the person can adjust. For seating, describe the position and support specifically while preserving their abilities and choice.

Agree on left and right from a reference such as the person’s perspective. “Here” or “over there” may be insufficient. Announce a change of guide beforehand and check who supports where before handing over; do not suddenly let go.

[Learning case] Pulling the person’s arm to hurry through a narrow doorway is inappropriate. Explain the narrowing beforehand and confirm preferred guidance and pace. Advance information allows adjustment of posture and stride.

This section explains reasons for assistance and what to check. Actual methods depend on the person’s condition, individual plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not attempt unfamiliar transfers or walking assistance from this text alone.

kaigo-move-07-words.heading: Vocabulary and useful expressions
paragraphs: 移動（いどう） — Mobility: moving between places for a purpose in everyday life.
予定表（よていひょう） — Schedule: planned activities and times. Distinguish it from a record of completed actions.
支援計画（しえんけいかく） — Support plan: arrangements for support based on the person’s goals and condition.
参加（さんか） — Participation: joining an activity. Distinguish available conditions from the person’s choice to join.
担当（たんとう） — Responsibility for supporting a person or carrying out assigned work.
確認（かくにん） — Checking: clarifying uncertainty by asking or observing directly.
ADL（エー・ディー・エル） — Basic activities of daily living, such as eating, dressing, toileting, bathing and mobility.
IADL（アイ・エー・ディー・エル） — Activities supporting life at home and in the community, such as shopping, money management and transport.
移乗（いじょう） — Transfer: changing the surface supporting the body, such as moving from bed to wheelchair.
移動用リフト（いどうようりふと） — Patient lift: equipment supporting and lifting the body to assist transfers. Check suitability and the trained method of use.
起き上がる（おきあがる） — To sit up: raising the upper body from lying toward sitting.
かける（かける） — In “apply the brakes,” this means activating the brakes to keep something stopped.
臥床（がしょう） — Lying in bed or on a similar surface.
車いす（くるまいす） — Wheelchair: equipment supporting seated mobility. It may be operated by the person or a helper.
声かけ（こえかけ） — Speaking to someone to explain, check, greet or otherwise communicate.
支える（ささえる） — To support: providing the support needed to keep a body or object stable.
シルバーカー（しるばーかー） — A walking cart for older people. Check each product’s purpose; do not assume it is a wheelchair.
高齢者用手押し車（こうれいしゃようておしぐるま） — A cart pushed by an older person. Check the product’s intended use rather than inferring from its name whether it can carry someone.
すべる（すべる） — To slide or slip: moving over a contacting surface, or losing secure footing.
スライディングシート（すらいでぃんぐしーと） — Sliding sheet: a sheet used to reduce friction when moving the body.
杖（つえ） — Cane: an aid providing additional support while walking. Check type and suitability.
つく（つく） — In “place a cane,” this means putting its tip on the floor or ground for support.
つかまる（つかまる） — To hold a rail or similar support to steady the body.
手すり（てすり） — Handrail: a fixture held for support when standing or walking.
握る（にぎる） — To grip: holding something by bending the fingers around it.
寝返り（ねがえり） — Turning over while lying down.
白杖（はくじょう） — White cane: used by a person with visual impairment to check surroundings and for related purposes. Respect their method of use.
ブレーキ（ぶれーき） — Brake: a device stopping or limiting wheel movement. Distinguish the roles and use of different types.
歩行器（ほこうき） — Walker: equipment supporting the body during walking. Check its type and use.
前屈み（まえかがみ） — Forward-leaning posture. The suitable degree depends on the person and action.
誘導（ゆうどう） — Guiding: explaining direction and path conditions according to the person’s wishes and condition.
床（ゆか） — Floor: a supporting surface in a room or passage. Check for moisture and objects.
離床（りしょう） — Getting out of bed to sit or take part in activities, according to the person’s condition and plan.
介護職（かいごしょく） — Care work: providing necessary daily assistance while respecting the person’s abilities and decisions.

kaigo-move-07-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Hasebe asks about the afternoon activity. The notice and internal message give different start times, so check with Kawase. Even once the time is known, participation wishes and mobility arrangements remain separate decisions.
Naoto Kawase: Is there anything you want to check about this afternoon?
Care worker Tanaka: The notice says two, but the message says two twenty. Which is current?
Naoto Kawase: Two twenty is current. It changed because of room preparations.
Care worker Tanaka: Understood. I’ve told Hasebe I’ll check and let them know.
Naoto Kawase: Please give them the new time. The person responsible will update the notice too.
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll check participation wishes and the support plan for that time before preparing to move.
Naoto Kawase: Please do. Ask me if anything about the mobility method is unclear.
Care worker Tanaka: Yes. I’ll first explain the change to two twenty and record what has been confirmed.

kaigo-move-07-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [New learning situation] The latest start is confirmed as 2:20 p.m. The notice remains unchanged, and the person has not yet been asked about participation after the change.
Give the new time and identify who updates the notice. Check wishes and the support plan for that time before preparing. Do not record uncompleted updates or consent as done.
Example: “The latest start is 2:20 p.m. The assigned person will update the notice. I’ll tell Hasebe, check participation wishes and the plan for that time, then prepare.”
Reflection: Did you distinguish updated information, work still to do and an unconfirmed personal choice?
